intro: All three are built on と言う, "to call something X". Each one takes the label X that has just been used and does something with it: というより swaps it for a better label, といっても lowers the expectations the label raises, and といえば uses it as a cue for what it brings to mind. Ask what the speaker is doing to the word X, and the choice follows.

skills.rule: X というより Y: "it is not so much X as Y"; X is not quite the right word, and Y is the more accurate one.
skills.explain:
というより corrects a description. X is partly true or is the word someone might expect, but the speaker finds Y fits better: 暖かいというより暑い (not so much warm as hot). Y is often reinforced with むしろ: 先生というより、むしろ友達だ.

It follows plain forms. Nouns and na-adjectives attach directly or with だ: 静かというより / 静かだというより, never 静かなというより. i-adjectives and verbs use the plain form: 疲れたというより. The casual spoken counterpart is というか.

The edge: X and Y lie on the same scale or describe the same thing from two angles, so X is not simply false. If reality is the opposite of X ("far from cheap, it was very expensive"), use どころか. If the speaker accepts X but limits it, use といっても.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は暖[あたた]かい{というより}暑[あつ]いです。
examples.en: Today it is not so much warm as hot.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]は友達[ともだち]{というより}家族[かぞく]のような人[ひと]です。
examples.en: He is less a friend than someone like family.

examples.jp: この部屋[へや]は静[しず]か{というより}寂[さび]しい感[かん]じがする。
examples.en: This room feels lonely rather than quiet.

examples.jp: 疲[つか]れた{というより}、少[すこ]し飽[あ]きてしまった。
examples.en: It is not so much that I am tired; I have got a bit bored.

examples.jp: 彼女[かのじょ]の話[はなし]は説明[せつめい]{というより}言[い]い訳[わけ]に聞[き]こえた。
examples.en: What she said sounded less like an explanation than an excuse.

contrast.note: どころか says reality is the opposite of X or goes far beyond it: 安いどころか高かった (far from cheap, it was expensive). というより only replaces X with a more fitting word on the same line.
といっても keeps X as true and then shrinks it: 休みといっても一日だけ. というより rejects X as the best word.

mistakes.bad: 安[やす]い{というより}、三倍[さんばい]も高[たか]かった。
mistakes.good: 安[やす]い{どころか}、三倍[さんばい]も高[たか]かった。
mistakes.note: The price was the opposite of cheap, not a more accurate version of it: use どころか.

mistakes.bad: 静[しず]かな{というより}寂[さび]しい。
mistakes.good: 静[しず]か{というより}寂[さび]しい。
mistakes.note: A na-adjective takes no な before というより; use the bare stem or add だ.

mistakes.bad: 休[やす]み{というより}、一日[いちにち]だけです。
mistakes.good: 休[やす]み{といっても}、一日[いちにち]だけです。
mistakes.note: It really is a holiday, just a short one: limiting X is といっても.

skills.tip: Can you say "not so much X as Y" in English? Then it is というより.

skills.rule: X といっても Y: "I say X, but don't imagine too much"; X is true, and Y cuts it down to its real size.
skills.explain:
といっても heads off the picture the word X creates. The speaker admits X and then adds the limiting fact: 料理ができるといっても、簡単なものだけです (I can cook, but only simple things). Y typically contains だけ, しか...ない, あまり...ない, or a small number.

It follows plain forms: nouns and na-adjectives attach directly or with だ (社長といっても / 社長だといっても), verbs and i-adjectives take the plain form, past included: 住んでいたといっても、半年だけ. In casual speech it becomes っていっても.

The edge: Y does not contradict X; it limits it. To reject a conclusion someone draws from X ("just because it is expensive does not mean it is good"), use からといって...とは限らない. To swap X for a better word, use というより.
patterns: [X] といっても、[only / not very / small number]
[plain verb, incl. past] といっても

examples.jp: 休[やす]み{といっても}、一日[いちにち]だけです。
examples.en: It is a holiday, but only for one day.

examples.jp: 料理[りょうり]ができる{といっても}、簡単[かんたん]なものだけです。
examples.en: I can cook, but only simple things.

examples.jp: 庭[にわ]がある{といっても}、とても狭[せま]いです。
examples.en: There is a garden, but it is very small.

examples.jp: 海外[かいがい]に住[す]んでいた{といっても}、半年[はんとし]だけです。
examples.en: I did live abroad, but only for half a year.

examples.jp: 社長[しゃちょう]{といっても}、社員[しゃいん]が三人[さんにん]しかいない小[ちい]さな会社[かいしゃ]です。
examples.en: I may be the company president, but it is a small company with only three employees.

contrast.note: からといって rejects an inference: 高いからといっていい物とは限らない (just because it is expensive does not mean it is good). といっても limits X itself.
というより says X is the wrong word. といっても says X is the right word but smaller than it sounds.
といえば uses X as a cue to bring up something associated with it, with no sense of "but".

mistakes.bad: 高[たか]い{といっても}、いい物[もの]とは限[かぎ]らない。
mistakes.good: 高[たか]い{からといって}、いい物[もの]とは限[かぎ]らない。
mistakes.note: Rejecting the conclusion "expensive, therefore good" is からといって...とは限らない.

mistakes.bad: 旅行[りょこう]{といえば}、近[ちか]くの温泉[おんせん]に一泊[いっぱく]しただけです。
mistakes.good: 旅行[りょこう]{といっても}、近[ちか]くの温泉[おんせん]に一泊[いっぱく]しただけです。
mistakes.note: "I say trip, but it was only one night" limits X, so it needs といっても.

skills.tip: If the next words are "but only ..." or "but not very ...", it is といっても.

skills.rule: X といえば Y: "speaking of X" or "when you say X, Y comes to mind"; X is a cue that calls up Y.
skills.explain:
といえば takes a word, often one that has just come up in conversation, and uses it to bring up something linked to it. Two common uses: naming the typical association (夏といえば花火 - say summer and you think of fireworks), and switching topic on the back of what someone said (山田さんといえば、結婚したそうですよ - speaking of Yamada, I hear he got married). Close variants are というと and といったら.

It attaches directly to nouns. With a question clause it means "if you ask whether X": 好きかといえば、そうでもない (if you ask whether I like it, not really). Here the answer usually goes against what the question suggests.

The edge: といえば never means "but". If the speaker is cutting X down to size, it is といっても. It is also not a neutral topic marker: for a plain statement about X, use は.
patterns: [word just mentioned] といえば、[new remark]

examples.jp: 夏[なつ]{といえば}、花火[はなび]ですね。
examples.en: When you think of summer, it is fireworks, isn't it?

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]の秋[あき]{といえば}、紅葉[こうよう]です。
examples.en: Say autumn in Japan, and you think of the autumn leaves.

examples.jp: 山田[やまだ]さん{といえば}、最近[さいきん]結婚[けっこん]したそうですよ。
examples.en: Speaking of Mr Yamada, I hear he got married recently.

examples.jp: 旅行[りょこう]{といえば}、来月[らいげつ]の予定[よてい]はもう決[き]まりましたか。
examples.en: Speaking of travel, have you decided on next month's plans yet?

examples.jp: 好[す]きか{といえば}、そうでもありません。
examples.en: If you ask whether I like it, not really.

contrast.note: といっても admits X and then limits it ("but only ..."). といえば uses X to call up an association, with no limiting.
にとって gives the person from whose standpoint something is judged: 私にとって大切だ. It does not introduce a topic by association.
としては means "as X" or "for X": 初心者としては上手だ (good for a beginner). It does not bring up a related idea.

mistakes.bad: 私[わたし]{といえば}、学生[がくせい]です。
mistakes.good: 私[わたし]{は}学生[がくせい]です。
mistakes.note: A plain statement about yourself needs は; といえば is for calling up an association.

mistakes.bad: 庭[にわ]がある{といえば}、とても狭[せま]いです。
mistakes.good: 庭[にわ]がある{といっても}、とても狭[せま]いです。
mistakes.note: "There is a garden, but it is tiny" limits X: use といっても.

skills.tip: If "speaking of X" or "say X and you think of ..." fits, it is といえば.
